source: Ratcliff & McKoon (2008) The diffusion decision model: theory and data for two-choice decision tasks
finding: Noisy evidence runs from a start point z to one of two bounds (0 and a). Drift rate v is set by stimulus quality. Bound separation a sets speed versus accuracy. Non-decision time Ter covers encoding and response.
numbers: Parameters: drift v, boundary a, start z, Ter, plus across-trial variability eta (drift SD), sz (start range), st (Ter range). Within-trial noise s is fixed as a scale. Fits use RT quantiles .1/.3/.5/.7/.9 with chi-square.
limits: Meant for fast single-stage decisions (mean RT under about 1000-1500 ms). Scaling parameter s is arbitrary. Only first 100k of 177k characters read.
agent_relevance: A stopping rule has two knobs: how fast evidence arrives (task difficulty) and how far the bound is (caution). Our agent controls only the bound.

source: Ratcliff & McKoon (2008) Exp 1-3 fits (human motion discrimination)
finding: Harder stimuli lowered drift only. Speed versus accuracy instructions changed the bound a and left Ter almost unchanged.
numbers: Exp1 N=15, 6 coherence levels 5-50%: accuracy .58-.94, mean RT about 660 to 550 ms, a=.111, drifts .042-.369. Exp2 N=14: a=.109 (speed) vs .152 (accuracy); median RT shifted 120-200 ms, accuracy only 0-6%. Exp3 N=17, 75:25 priors: bias was mostly a start-point shift (about one third toward the likely bound).
limits: Averaged-subject chi-square is for relative comparison only. Human RT distributions are right-skewed, unlike near-symmetric monkey ones.
agent_relevance: Raising the bound bought little accuracy (0-6 points) for a large time cost (120-200 ms). Expect diminishing returns from extra samples.

source: Ratcliff & McKoon (2008) correct versus error RT
finding: Drift variability across trials makes errors slower than correct answers. Start-point variability makes errors faster. Both together explain both patterns, even reversals within one experiment.
numbers: Difficulty moves the .9 vs .1 RT quantile spread about 4:1. Speed-accuracy manipulations move the whole distribution about 2:1.
limits: Needs the extra variability parameters to fit; the plain Wald-style model cannot.
agent_relevance: Samples that disagree late may mean a hard item, not a wrong run. Time to agree is itself a difficulty signal.

source: Ratcliff (1978) A theory of memory retrieval, Psychological Review 85:59-108
finding: First diffusion model of two-choice decisions. Evidence is a continuous random walk to bounds. It gave full RT distributions for correct and error responses.
numbers: No numbers recorded (not opened this session).
limits: Not opened; claim from background knowledge. Original applied to memory retrieval.
agent_relevance: Founding source for treating the count of attempts as a bounded accumulation.

source: Wald (1945) Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses; Wald & Wolfowitz (1948) optimum character of the SPRT
finding: SPRT: add the log-likelihood ratio of each observation and stop when it crosses an upper or lower bound. Wald and Wolfowitz proved it needs the fewest samples on average for given error rates.
numbers: Bounds approx log((1-b)/a) and log(b/(1-a)) for error rates a, b (background knowledge, not checked).
limits: Not opened. Optimality holds for known, independent, identically distributed evidence.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the agent: stop when accumulated log-odds of an answer pass a bound. Independence is exactly what LLM samples lack (guardrail G4).

source: Gold & Shadlen (2007) The neural basis of decision making, Annu Rev Neurosci 30:535-574
finding: Review of the claim that sensory neurons (MT) supply momentary evidence and parietal LIP neurons accumulate its difference until a bound. Accumulation is read as log-likelihood ratio computation.
numbers: Page fetch returned 403; no numbers verified.
limits: Not opened (publisher blocked access). Framing is theirs; later work (a11, a12) disputes parts of it.
agent_relevance: Supports a program-side counter plus bound as the stopping rule, with evidence given as log-odds, not raw votes.

source: Roitman & Shadlen (2002) Response of neurons in LIP during a combined visual discrimination reaction time task
finding: In a free-response random-dot task, LIP firing ramped up at a rate that grew with motion strength. Just before the saccade the rate reached a common level whatever the coherence.
numbers: 2 monkeys, 54 LIP neurons, 6 coherences 0-51.2%. Mean correct RT 824 ms at 0% down to 409 ms at 51.2%. Ramp slope scaled 21.5 to 88.8 spikes/s^2. Pre-saccade rate 68.6 +/- 0.9 spikes/s with no coherence effect (p=0.46). At 6.4% coherence slope was 53.4 (short RT) vs 33.9 (long RT) spikes/s^2.
limits: Two monkeys. Monkey RT distributions are near symmetric, unlike human. Threshold seen for the preferred choice only; opposite choice stayed coherence dependent. Last 34k characters unread.
agent_relevance: Core biological evidence for a fixed commitment level reached sooner on easy items: the number of samples used should vary by item, not be fixed.

source: Kiani, Hanks & Shadlen (2008) Bounded integration in parietal cortex underlies decisions even when viewing duration is dictated by the environment
finding: Even when viewing time was fixed by the experimenter, monkeys behaved as if they stopped integrating when a bound was hit. Early motion pulses swayed choices, late pulses did not.
numbers: 2 monkeys, 51 LIP neurons, 42,647 trials. Motion 80-1500 ms. Bounded accumulation k=0.46, B=19.9 beat leaky accumulation (BIC favoured bounded, Bayes factor 8.35e12). Accuracy saturated beyond about 420 ms. Pulse shift 1.3 +/- 0.1% coherence (p<1e-8). Bound crossing time correlated with RT (r=0.16).
limits: Bound explanation vs leak is model-based. Correlation of crossing time with RT is weak (r=0.16).
agent_relevance: Evidence after the bound is wasted: late samples add nothing once a stop has been reached, so a stop rule should not be second-guessed by later samples.

source: Hanks, Mazurek, Kiani, Hopp & Shadlen (2011) Elapsed decision time affects the weighting of prior probability
finding: Prior odds are not a fixed start-point shift. A bias signal that grows with elapsed time fits better. Longer deliberation leans more on the prior.
numbers: 2 humans (2,400-3,125 trials per condition) and 4 monkeys (36,687 trials; 52 LIP neurons from 2). Dynamic bias beat static start-point model: Bayes factor >1e8 humans, >1e6 monkeys. Fitted prior weight phi 0.88/0.85 (humans), 0.80 +/- 0.01 (monkeys). Under speed pressure bias rose 5.1% to 10.8% and 4.1% to 8.3% coherence. Collapsing bounds did not rescue the static model (BF >1e6).
limits: Very small human N (two people). Monkeys heavily trained.
agent_relevance: Priors (base rates) should weigh in more the longer an item stays unresolved, and should be applied by code as a time-growing term.

source: Hanks, Kiani & Shadlen (2014) A neural mechanism of speed-accuracy tradeoff in macaque area LIP, eLife
finding: Speed pressure did not lower the firing-rate threshold. It added an evidence-independent signal that pushes activity toward the fixed threshold (an urgency or start-point shift).
numbers: 2 monkeys, 70 LIP neurons (35 per regime), 3,307-4,838 trials per monkey per regime. RT 176 +/- 4 ms and 159 +/- 3 ms longer under accuracy regime. Evidence needed 43% +/- 2% smaller under speed. Threshold did not differ (p>0.5). Model R2 0.99 and 0.97.
limits: Two monkeys. Contradicts the simple 'lower the bound' reading of speed-accuracy trade-off.
agent_relevance: Two ways to be hurried: lower the bar, or add a free time-based push. The second means stopping earlier with less real evidence; the agent should log which it uses.

source: Hawkins, Forstmann, Wagenmakers, Ratcliff & Brown (2015) Revisiting the evidence for collapsing boundaries and urgency signals in perceptual decision-making
finding: A large reanalysis found most human data favour a fixed bound, not a collapsing bound or urgency signal. Support for dynamic bounds comes mostly from monkeys and from highly practiced or delayed-feedback paradigms.
numbers: 9 datasets, 8 studies, 3 paradigms, 4 labs; 85 humans and 8 macaques, over 116,000 decisions. Humans: 72/85 fixed, 9 collapsing, 4 inconclusive. Monkeys: 4/8 collapsing, 2 fixed, 2 urgency. Urgency model best for 3 of 93. Replication on 91 more human datasets: 64 strong fixed (P>=.99), 12 fixed (.95-.99), 1 collapsing, 14 no preference.
limits: Result depends on paradigm, practice, feedback delay, and on including between-trial variability. Collapsing bounds are hard to tell from variability.
agent_relevance: A constant stopping threshold is the safe default. Do not add a time-decaying threshold without evidence in our own task.

source: Drugowitsch, Moreno-Bote, Churchland, Shadlen & Pouget (2012) The cost of accumulating evidence in perceptual decision making
finding: If reward rate is maximised and difficulty varies, the best bound shrinks over time, even with a constant cost per second. The fitted cost of time was neither zero nor constant.
numbers: 2 monkeys (2,615 and 3,534 trials), 6 humans (about 562 trials each); coherences 0-51.2%. Monkey R2 0.987. AIC for the cost model -809 and 620 vs 26,436 and 48,006 for a constant-bound model (monkeys). Humans mean R2 0.961. LIP urgency was the same across coherences, as predicted.
limits: Partly opposes a11. Gain over constant bound shows mainly in RT distributions and error RTs, not mean accuracy. Corrected in 2015 erratum (J Neurosci 35:15477). Text beyond 100k characters unread.
agent_relevance: When item difficulty varies and attempts have a cost, the best stop point relaxes with time: give up sooner on items that stay unresolved. Test it, given a11.

source: Palmer, Huk & Shadlen (2005) The effect of stimulus strength on the speed and accuracy of a perceptual decision, J Vision 5:376-404
finding: Human motion-coherence data across strengths fitted by bounded accumulation. Named in a11 as one dataset favouring dynamic bounds.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened; seen only second-hand via a11.
agent_relevance: Another dataset where a bounded-accumulation fit works across difficulty levels.

source: Bogacz, Brown, Moehlis, Holmes & Cohen (2006) The physics of optimal decision making, Psychological Review 113:700-765
finding: Showed the diffusion model is the continuous limit of the SPRT for two choices, hence optimal; leaky competing accumulators reduce to it when inhibition balances leak.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened (PMC fetch returned an unrelated paper). Optimality is for two alternatives only.
agent_relevance: Gives a theory-backed route from two answers to the SPRT. For more than two answers the optimum is not a simple race.

source: Usher & McClelland (2001) The time course of perceptual choice: the leaky, competing accumulator model, Psychological Review 108:550-592
finding: Accumulators for each option leak and inhibit each other. Handles more than two choices and gives recency effects.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened. Leak was not supported over a bound in a08 (bounded beat leaky).
agent_relevance: Multi-answer version: a vote tally where rival answers inhibit each other.

source: Brown & Heathcote (2008) The simplest complete model of choice response time: linear ballistic accumulation, Cognitive Psychology 57:153-178
finding: Race of noise-free linear accumulators, with variability only between trials. Fits RT and choice with fewer assumptions.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows that a race model without within-trial noise is enough; LLM samples are whole independent runs, so a race of counters is the natural fit.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang & Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency (EMNLP 2023)
finding: Sample answers one at a time. Stop when a Beta test says the leading answer is the majority with probability above a threshold (0.95). This is a Bayesian sequential stopping rule over answer counts.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs, temperature 0.7, cap 40. Maths: 73.2 to 73.1 accuracy with 40 to 13.8 generations (3.3x fewer). Commonsense 66.0 to 65.8, 15.8 gens (2.9x). Symbolic 72.8 to 72.8, 13.1 gens (3.8x). Code 35.2 to 35.6, 312.5 to 173.6 (2.4x). GPT-3.5-turbo 76.4 to 76.2, 10.0 gens (4.4x); Vicuna-13B 54.0 to 54.1, 21.7 gens (1.9x). Up to 7.9x on Boolean expressions.
limits: Threshold 0.95 fixed for all tasks. At equal average cost (10 samples) about 3% higher accuracy on GSM8K than fixed self-consistency. Assumes the sampled answers are exchangeable draws, which is not strictly true.
agent_relevance: The closest working analogue to the SPRT for attempts. A Beta stopping rule is cheap (0.03 ms) and can be coded directly.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) stopping-rule comparison
finding: Six stopping rules were compared: random, majority, entropy, Beta, Dirichlet, Chinese restaurant process. Beta beat entropy and majority at the same cost. Dirichlet and CRP matched Beta but were far slower.
numbers: Beta/entropy 0.03 ms; Dirichlet 101.3 ms; CRP 94.6 ms (about 4 orders of magnitude). Naive 'stop at majority' mostly under-performed. SVAMP needs fewer than 5 samples on average.
limits: Thresholds tuned on the same benchmarks they report; no held-out threshold test seen in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Do not stop at a bare majority. Use a probability-of-majority test, not a vote count.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ICLR 2024)
finding: Sample in windows of w. Stop when all answers in a window are identical (zero-entropy window). A control scheme sets w and the max L from the first window.
numbers: Window w=8 for MATH, 5 for others. Average sampling reduction vs self-consistency: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. GPT-3.5: accuracy within -0.02 to -0.85 points of SC (e.g. GSM8K 85.69 to 85.67). GSM8K cost $0.0084 SC vs $0.0052 ESC (GPT-3.5); $0.1501 adaptive-consistency vs $0.0769 ESC on GPT-4.
limits: Conservative rule needs a whole window to agree; sampling in windows shares prompt tokens. Averaged over 10 runs. Savings smallest on hard sets (MATH).
agent_relevance: A window rule is a simple, tuning-free stopping rule; costs less than one-by-one sampling when prompts are long.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Make Every Penny Count: Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (NAACL Findings)
finding: Most questions do not gain from self-consistency, so pre-rank difficulty and give easy items one sample. Sequential stopping rules still waste samples on easy questions and add input cost.
numbers: Only 3.8% of questions (GPT-4) benefit from SC over a single CoT. DSC cuts cost vs SC by 65.29% (GPT-4) and 56.04% (GPT-3.5-turbo); vs ESC by 24.81% and 21.86%. Six benchmarks.
limits: Needs a batch of questions and an LLM difficulty ranking, which adds its own cost. Read in part (introduction and results summary).
agent_relevance: Adds a prior over difficulty before the first sample: a counterpart to the prior term in a09.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian & Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Use token-level group confidence to kill weak reasoning traces mid-generation, and stop sampling more traces when the leading answer reaches a consensus share.
numbers: Offline: 99.9% on AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B at 512 traces vs 97.0% majority and 91.8% pass@1. Online: up to 84.7% fewer tokens. Warm-up 16 traces. Qwen3-32B on AIME24 with consensus threshold 0.95: accuracy unchanged and tokens down 15.4%/52.8% (B=32/512, low) and 22.0%/54.7% (high). Threshold 0.85-0.90 saves up to 69.6% but loses up to 0.47 points (low variant).
limits: Savings depend on the budget cap (adaptive stop only after 16 warm-up traces). Best threshold varies by model and dataset. Needs token log-probs.
agent_relevance: Two stops combine: per-attempt abort on low confidence plus an across-attempt consensus stop. Needs probability access.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Inside one long chain of thought, probe a trial answer at reasoning transitions. Stop thinking when the trial answer confidence is high enough. About 75% of samples contain an earlier correct exit point.
numbers: 11 reasoning LLMs, 10 benchmarks. CoT length cut 19.1% to 80.1%, accuracy up 0.3 to 5.0 points. 60.8% and 35.1% of correct outcomes can be reached with only 20% of reasoning steps (as reported in the paper's Fig 2a analysis; dataset split not checked). Best exit at 40% of steps on MATH, 50% on GPQA.
limits: Stopping inside one chain is within-attempt, not across attempts. Confidence from the model's own token probabilities. Only the introduction and analysis section were read.
agent_relevance: Same bound idea applied to the depth of a single attempt: a within-attempt stopping rule to pair with the across-attempt rule.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Fixed-size sampling then majority vote is the baseline that all stopping rules above try to shorten.
numbers: Reported gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9 points (abstract only).
limits: Abstract page only; full text not read. Fixed sample count per question.
agent_relevance: Baseline for any stopping-rule saving claim.

source: Synthesis: fixed vs collapsing bound dispute (a11, a12)
finding: Hawkins 2015 (humans mostly fixed bound) and Drugowitsch 2012 (optimal theory and monkeys: collapsing bound) disagree. Paradigm, practice, feedback delay and variability parameters decide the result.
numbers: a11: 72 of 85 humans fixed. a12: optimal bound collapses under variable difficulty.
limits: Both rest on model comparison, not direct observation of the bound. This line is our own synthesis, not a source.
agent_relevance: Use a fixed confidence bound as default with a hard cap on attempts; test a relaxing bound only if our item difficulty varies widely.

source: Synthesis: independence assumption in LLM stopping rules (a05, a17, a19)
finding: The SPRT and the Beta test treat each sample as an independent draw. LLM samples are correlated, so a stated 0.95 confidence is optimistic. The papers still saw small accuracy losses on benchmarks, but benchmarks are where samples often agree easily.
numbers: Observed accuracy drops: -0.1 (maths) and -0.2 (commonsense) points at 0.95 in a17; -0.02 to -0.85 in a19.
limits: Sources read did not test stopping when a model is confidently wrong in a shared way. This line is our own synthesis, not a source.
agent_relevance: Agreement stop is a hint only (G4). Add a held-out check (G3) before committing even after the bound is crossed.
